title: A book that sorts true from false, sent piece by piece.
subtitle: Why the Quran is called the Criterion

row.title: verse after verse
sub: a sign of care for the receiver

then: In Makkah, people were arguing about the Quran and about the Prophet ﷺ. The surah opens by praising Allah for sending it. Ibn Kathir notes the verb means {idea}sent down often, in stages{/idea}, unlike earlier books. And the Prophet ﷺ is called {reward}His servant{/reward}, a title of honor.
now: You scroll through ten opinions on the same question before lunch. Everyone sounds sure. You close the app more confused than when you opened it. {idea}A criterion is a measuring stick{/idea}, something you hold every opinion up against, including your own.
old: Truth is whatever sounds most confident today.
new: Allah gave a fixed measure, and I can test things against it.
try: Next time you feel pulled by a strong opinion online, pause and ask: what would the Quran weigh this against?

title: He owns it all and measured every thing to fit.
subtitle: No partner, no son, and nothing made by accident

row.title: measured
sub: created, then sized to its role

then: The Quran was answering people who gave Allah partners and children. Ibn Kathir explains that {idea}everything apart from Him is created and subject to Him{/idea}. He made each thing and set its measure exactly.
now: You look at your life and some parts feel badly sized: the small flat, the slow career, the body that tires early. You assume it is all luck. {idea}The verse says each thing was measured.{/idea} That does not mean stop trying. It means nothing in your life is outside His control.
old: My life is a pile of accidents I have to manage alone.
new: The One who measured everything also measured my portion, and He has no rival.
try: Pick one thing in your life you resent the size of. Say: He measured this, and ask Him for good in it.

title: They worshipped things that cannot even help themselves.
subtitle: Gods that create nothing and are created
then: The people of Makkah kept idols as gods beside Allah. Ibn Kathir calls this the ignorance of the idolators: {trap}idols who could not create the wing of a gnat{/trap}, yet were treated as if they could protect their worshippers. Only Allah gives life, takes it, and brings everyone back.
now: Your mood depends on a number in your bank app. Or on one person's approval. Or on the boss liking your last email. These are not idols of stone, but you check them the way a worshipper checks a shrine. {idea}None of them can keep themselves alive, let alone you.{/idea}
old: If I keep this person or this money on my side, I am safe.
new: Anything that cannot save itself cannot save me. Only the Living One can.
try: Notice the one thing you check most anxiously today. Each time, say quietly: this is created, Allah is the One I rely on.

title: They called it a lie and knew they were lying.
subtitle: The first accusation: he made it up with help
then: Quraysh had known the Prophet ﷺ for about forty years and called him {reward}Al-Amin, the Trustworthy{/reward}. When the message came, they suddenly called it an invention made with outside help. Ibn Kathir says {trap}their own souls knew{/trap} the claim was not true.
now: A colleague gets the promotion you wanted. Last week you praised their work. This week you are telling a friend they probably had help, or charm, or luck. {idea}The story changed when your interest did.{/idea}
old: I am just being realistic about how they really got there.
new: When my opinion of someone flips the moment they threaten me, the problem is in me.
try: Think of one person you have recently talked down. Say one true good thing about them to someone today.

title: Old stories, they said, read to him morning and evening.
subtitle: The second accusation, and why it falls apart
then: The next charge was that the Quran was old legends someone wrote down and recited to him all day. Ibn Kathir points out that it was {idea}well known he never learned to read or write{/idea}. They knew him for forty years. {trap}They could not settle on one accusation.{/trap}
now: Someone you dislike posts something wise. Your first move is to search for where they copied it from. You are not curious about the idea, only about how to dismiss it. {idea}Looking for a way out is different from looking for the truth.{/idea}
old: If I can find a reason to dismiss it, I do not have to think about it.
new: Rushing to explain a truth away is a sign I do not want it to be true.
try: Take one idea you rejected because of who said it. Give it five honest minutes on its own merits.

title: The reply to slander ends with an open door.
subtitle: He knows every secret, and still forgives
then: After the accusations, Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to answer: it comes from the One who {idea}knows the secret of the heavens and the earth{/idea}. Then He calls Himself Forgiving and Merciful. Ibn Kathir says this is {reward}an invitation to repent{/reward}, offered to the very people slandering him.
now: You said something cruel in the family group chat last year. Everyone remembers. You feel you have used up your chance. {reward}This verse was spoken to people far worse{/reward}, and it still ended with: He forgives.
old: After what I have said and done, the door is closed for me.
new: He knows the secret I hide, and He still calls Himself Forgiving to me.
try: Make one quiet, honest request for forgiveness for something you thought was too big.

title: He eats and shops in markets, so how is he a messenger?
subtitle: The objection that a prophet looked too ordinary
then: Quraysh saw the Prophet ﷺ eat as they ate and {idea}go to the markets to trade and earn{/idea}. They asked why no angel came down to stand beside him. Ibn Kathir compares it to {trap}Pharaoh asking why Musa had no gold bracelets or angels{/trap}.
now: You dismiss the imam because he drives an old car. You doubt the teacher because you saw her shopping in slippers. {idea}You expect truth to arrive dressed up.{/idea} Often it comes from someone queuing next to you.
old: Someone that ordinary cannot have anything important to tell me.
new: An ordinary life is exactly where a real message is meant to be lived.
try: Listen fully today to someone you usually overlook because they seem too ordinary.

title: No treasure, no garden, so they called him bewitched.
subtitle: Judging truth by wealth
then: They kept asking for proof they could hold: {reward}a treasure to spend, a garden to eat from{/reward}. When none came, the wrongdoers told the believers they were following a man under a spell. Ibn Kathir notes all of this was easy for Allah, but {idea}He had a reason for not doing it{/idea}.
now: You trust the finance influencer with the rented sports car more than your quiet uncle who has never been in debt. {trap}The display wins the argument.{/trap} Ask what you are actually measuring.
old: If someone is right, it should show in their success.
new: Wealth is not a proof of truth, and its absence is not a proof of falsehood.
try: When you next judge a person by what they own, stop and name one thing about their character instead.

title: So many labels, and none of them led anywhere.
subtitle: When you keep switching your excuse

key.label: Why they could not find a path

then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to look at how they keep inventing comparisons for him. Ibn Kathir lists them: {trap}a sorcerer, bewitched, crazy, a liar, a poet{/trap}. He says {idea}the truth is one{/idea}, and whoever leaves it is lost no matter which way he goes.
now: You skipped the prayer. First it was work. Then you were tired. Then it was too late anyway. Each excuse replaced the last. {idea}When reasons keep changing, the real reason is not on the list.{/idea}
old: I have a good reason each time.
new: Changing excuses usually hide one thing I do not want to admit.
try: Pick one thing you keep putting off. Write your real reason in one honest line.

title: He could give you gardens and palaces if He willed.
subtitle: What they asked for is small to Allah

picture.label: What they demanded vs what He could give

then: To the demand for a treasure and a garden, Allah replies that He could give the Prophet ﷺ {reward}better than all that, gardens and palaces{/reward}. Mujahid said this means in this world. Quraysh called every stone house a palace. {idea}It was never a question of power.{/idea}
now: Your friend got the house, the car, the wedding. You are still renting and praying. You start to wonder if Allah forgot you. {idea}What you are waiting for is tiny to Him.{/idea} Its delay is not His inability.
old: If Allah loved me, I would have what they have by now.
new: He could give me far more in a moment. The timing is His wisdom, not His limit.
try: Make one dua today for the thing you want, and add: if it is good for me.

title: The real problem was not him. It was the Hour.
subtitle: What sat underneath all their objections
then: After all the demands, the verse names the root: {trap}they denied the Hour{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says they were not asking to find guidance. Their disbelief in the Day of Resurrection is what made them say it. A blaze is prepared for those who deny it.
now: You argue with every reminder about prayer, debt, or how you speak to your parents. Each time it is a different detail. {idea}Underneath, it may be that the Day just does not feel real to you right now.{/idea}
old: I just have honest questions about the details.
new: Sometimes my questions are a way to avoid believing that this all gets counted.
try: Spend two minutes tonight picturing standing before Allah. Then ask what you would change tomorrow.

title: The Fire is heard from far away.
subtitle: The warning reaches them before they arrive

row.title: now, from far
sub: this verse is the distant sound

then: The verse describes the Fire seeing the deniers {trap}from a far place{/trap}, the place of gathering, and they hear its raging. Ibn Kathir cites a report from Ibn Abbas of people pulled toward it, and some being released when they said {reward}they had hoped for His mercy{/reward}.
now: A doctor tells you to change your diet now, years before anything breaks. Most of us wait for the alarm. {idea}This verse is the warning heard from far off{/idea}, while there is still time to turn around.
old: I will deal with it when it gets close.
new: The warning is given from far away so I can turn back long before.
try: Choose one habit you know is harming you and take one small step away from it today.

title: In a narrow place, they cry out for an end.
subtitle: Regret when nothing can be undone
then: The verse describes the deniers placed in {trap}a narrow place, bound{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says they will utter cries of woe, regret and sorrow. It is told to Makkans who still had their whole lives to respond.
now: Lying awake, you replay something you did. The feeling is heavy. {reward}That ache today is a mercy{/reward}, because you can still act on it: apologize, repay, pray. The verse shows regret that has nowhere to go.
old: Feeling guilty is just a bad feeling I should push away.
new: Regret I feel today is a gift, because I can still do something with it.
try: Take one regret that visits you often and do one small thing to repair it.

title: Not one cry of ruin, but many.
subtitle: The reply to their cry of regret

row.title: many
sub: the loss is bigger than one cry

then: Those who cried out for destruction are answered: {trap}do not cry for one destruction today, but for many{/trap}. Their regret will not end their situation. It closes the scene that began with denying the Hour.
now: You tell yourself one more late night of that habit is just one. But it is never just one. {idea}Small choices stack up quietly{/idea}, and the verse shows a total no one can carry. The good news: good choices stack too.
old: It is only this once, it will not add up.
new: Choices add up, so each small one matters, the good ones as well.
try: Replace one small repeated bad choice today with a good one, and do it again tomorrow.

title: Is that better, or the Garden that lasts forever?
subtitle: A simple question placed after the warning
then: Right after the scene of the Fire, Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to ask: {idea}is that better, or the Garden of Eternity?{/idea} Ibn Kathir says it is prepared {reward}as a reward and final destination{/reward} for those with taqwa, in return for their obedience. He compares it to a similar question in Surah As-Saffat.
now: Payday comes. You can spend it all on this weekend or set some aside for something that lasts. You already know which is wiser, you just need someone to ask the question out loud. {idea}This verse asks it.{/idea}
old: The reward is far away and vague; today is real.
new: When I put both endings side by side, the choice becomes obvious.
try: Before one decision today, ask yourself plainly: which of these lasts?

title: Whatever they wish, forever, as a binding promise.
subtitle: A promise from Allah that is owed

row.title: a promise He binds Himself to

then: After describing the Fire, the surah describes the Garden: {reward}all that they desire, forever{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says the phrase means {idea}a binding pledge that must come to pass{/idea}. The pious may ask Him for it, because He promised.
now: Your manager promised a raise next year and you have heard that before. People make promises they cannot keep. {idea}This one is made by the only One who never breaks His word{/idea}, and you are invited to ask for it.
old: Promises disappoint, so I keep my hopes low.
new: This is one promise I can hold Allah to, so I can hope fully.
try: Ask Allah for Paradise by name in one of your prayers today.

title: Did they mislead you, or did you wander off yourselves?
subtitle: The worshipped are questioned in front of the worshippers
then: On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will gather the idolators with those they worshipped. Mujahid said this includes {idea}Isa, Uzayr and the angels{/idea}. He will ask the worshipped: did you call them to this, or {trap}was it their own idea{/trap}? Ibn Kathir compares it to the question put to Isa in 5:116.
now: You picked up a habit because your circle did it. You quietly plan to say "everyone around me was doing it." {idea}The verse imagines that circle being asked{/idea}, and you hearing their answer.
old: If I followed others, the blame is mostly theirs.
new: The ones I follow will be asked about me, and they may say I chose this myself.
try: Name one thing you do mainly because others around you do it. Decide if you would choose it alone.

title: Comfort lasted so long they forgot the reminder.
subtitle: How easy lives drift from the message
then: The worshipped reply: {idea}glory be to You, it was not for us to take protectors besides You{/idea}. They did not call anyone to worship them. Ibn Kathir explains the rest: {trap}a long time of comfort passed{/trap}, and people forgot what the messengers brought.
now: Everything is fine. Salary in, kids healthy, weekends full. Weeks pass without a real prayer or a page of Quran, and nothing feels wrong. {trap}Comfort rarely pulls you away all at once. It lets you forget slowly.{/trap}
old: Things are going well, so I must be doing fine with Allah.
new: Ease is exactly when I am most likely to forget, so it needs more remembering.
try: On a good day this week, stop for one minute and thank Allah for a specific comfort by name.

title: The ones they relied on will deny them.
subtitle: Protectors who turn into witnesses against

row.title: only Allah
sub: the rest cannot even help themselves

then: The worshipped {trap}will show their worshippers to be liars{/trap} in claiming they were helpers who brought them close to Allah. Ibn Kathir links it to 46:5-6, where those called on become enemies. Then a warning: {idea}whoever does wrong among you{/idea} will taste a great punishment.
now: You cut corners at work because a senior colleague said it was fine. Then the audit comes and he says he never said that. {trap}People you lean on in wrong things tend to step away when it counts.{/trap}
old: If someone important approves, I am covered.
new: No one I lean on in wrong will stand with me when it matters.
try: If you are doing something only because someone said it is fine, check it yourself today.

title: Every messenger ate food and walked in markets.
subtitle: The answer to verse 7, and a test for all of us

key.label: Why people differ in their lives

then: This answers the objection from verse 7. Ibn Kathir says {idea}all the earlier messengers ate and went to markets to earn a living{/idea}. Then: We made some of you a trial for others, will you be patient? He notes the Prophet ﷺ was offered to be a king-prophet and {reward}chose to be a servant and messenger{/reward}.
now: Your neighbor's son got the scholarship. Your sister's husband earns twice what yours does. You feel tested by other people's lives. {idea}The verse says that is exactly the test{/idea}, and your Lord is watching how you hold it.
old: Other people's good fortune is unfair to me.
new: Other people are part of my test, and patience with that is seen by Allah.
try: Think of someone whose life makes you feel smaller. Make one sincere dua for them today.

title: Show us angels, show us our Lord, they demanded.
subtitle: When demands are really pride

row.title: do not expect to meet Him
pride
sub: they thought too highly of themselves

then: People who did not expect to meet Allah asked for angels to come down to them, or {trap}to see their Lord directly{/trap}. Ibn Kathir links it to their demand in 17:92. Allah's verdict: {trap}they think too highly of themselves{/trap} and are scornful with great pride.
now: You tell a friend you will start praying properly once you get a clear sign. Then a sign comes and you ask for a clearer one. {trap}Sometimes the bar keeps rising because you do not want to move.{/trap}
old: I will believe and act once I get the proof I asked for.
new: Setting the terms for Allah is pride, even when it sounds like reasonable doubt.
try: Notice one condition you have set before you will change something. Drop it and take one step.

title: They will see the angels, but not as they hoped.
subtitle: The request granted at the worst moment
then: They demanded to see angels. Ibn Kathir explains they will, {trap}at death and on the Day of Resurrection{/trap}, and it will bring no good news to them. The angels will say success is forbidden to them. He contrasts the believers, to whom the angels say {reward}fear not, nor grieve{/reward}, from 41:30.
now: Some people want to be proven right so badly they forget what being proven right might cost. {idea}The same angels can arrive with comfort or with bad news{/idea}, and it depends on how you lived before they came.
old: I want to see it with my own eyes before I take it seriously.
new: By the time I see it, it will be too late to prepare. I want them to greet me with good news.
try: Read 41:30 today and ask Allah to make you among those the angels comfort.

title: Their deeds become dust floating in a sunbeam.
subtitle: Work that had no sincere root

row.title: scattered dust
sub: specks in a ray of sun

then: On the Day of Resurrection, Allah turns to the deeds the idolators thought would save them. Ibn Kathir says a deed counts when it is {idea}sincere and in line with what Allah set out{/idea}. Ali explained the dust as {trap}specks seen in the sun's rays through a small opening{/trap}.
now: You helped at the charity drive and posted the photo. You gave, and made sure people knew. {idea}A sunbeam through the window shows how much dust is in the air{/idea}. Ask which of your deeds would hold weight if no one ever saw them.
old: As long as I do good things, how and why I do them does not matter much.
new: A good deed lasts when it is done sincerely for Allah, not for an audience.
try: Do one good thing today that nobody will ever know about.

title: That Day, the people of the Garden have the best home.
subtitle: A place to settle and a place to rest
then: Right after deeds turn to dust for the arrogant, the verse turns to the people of the Garden. That Day they have {reward}the best abode and the fairest place of repose{/reward}. The contrast is placed side by side, as the surah does again and again.
now: You come home after a twelve-hour shift and just want to sit somewhere quiet. Everyone knows that longing. {reward}The verse promises a settlement and a rest{/reward} that no shift will end.
old: Rest is something I will get when I retire, maybe.
new: The truest rest is waiting for those who lived for Allah.
try: Tonight, before sleeping, ask Allah for the best resting place in the Hereafter.

title: The sky splits with clouds and angels pour down.
subtitle: The Day when everything comes to judgment
then: They had asked for angels to be sent down. Here the angels do come down, on the Day of Resurrection, when {idea}the heaven is split by clouds{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says the angels will {idea}surround all creatures at the place of gathering{/idea}, and then judgment begins.
now: Sitting in traffic, you look at the sky and it just looks like weather. {idea}This verse asks you to picture that same sky opening{/idea}, with no traffic, no phones, only you and what you did.
old: The sky above me is just the background to my day.
new: The same sky will one day open, and I will stand in front of my Lord.
try: Next time you look up at the sky today, remember this Day for one breath.

title: That Day, all rule belongs to the Most Merciful.
subtitle: No kings, no tyrants, one Sovereign

row.title: safe
sub: the great terror does not grieve them

then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in which Allah folds the heavens and says: {idea}I am the Sovereign, where are the kings of the earth?{/idea} The Day is hard for the disbelievers because it is the Day of justice. For the believers, he quotes 21:103: {reward}the greatest terror will not grieve them{/reward}.
now: The person who controls your schedule, your visa, your pay seems very powerful today. {idea}Their power is borrowed, and it ends.{/idea} And the One who rules that Day calls Himself the Most Merciful.
old: The people with power over my life decide my fate.
new: All power returns to the Most Merciful, and He is the One I answer to.
try: When someone's power over you makes you anxious today, say quietly: the kingdom belongs to the Most Merciful.

title: Biting his hands: if only I had walked with the Messenger.
subtitle: The regret of the one who chose another path

row.title: if only
sub: I had taken a path with him

then: Ibn Kathir describes the regret of {trap}the wrongdoer who rejected the path of the Messenger{/trap}. He says it may have been revealed about Uqbah bin Abi Mu'it or another, but {idea}it applies to every wrongdoer{/idea}. On that Day the regret will avail him nothing.
now: You know which path you should be on. You keep saying next month. {reward}The verse is a voice from the future{/reward}, letting you hear the if only while you can still act on it.
old: There is plenty of time to get serious later.
new: I would rather feel the pull of this verse today than say if only on that Day.
try: Pick one practice of the Prophet ﷺ you have neglected and do it once today.

title: Woe to me, I wish I had never befriended him.
subtitle: The friend who pulled you away
then: The wrongdoer names his regret: {trap}a close friend{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says this is the one among the callers to misguidance who diverted him from guidance, {idea}whether Umayyah bin Khalaf, his brother Ubayy, or someone else{/idea}. The verse leaves the name blank.
now: The friend who always says skip it, one time is fine. The group that makes fun of you for praying. You laugh along. {idea}The verse leaves the name blank so you can fill it in{/idea}, and also ask whose blank you might be.
old: My friends do not really change who I am.
new: The people closest to me are shaping where I end up.
try: Spend time this week with one friend who makes you better, and tell them so.

title: He led me away after the reminder had reached me.
subtitle: And Satan always walks away in the end
then: The regret goes on: {trap}he led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says the Reminder is the Quran. Then the verse adds that Satan is {trap}a deserter{/trap}: he leads man from the truth and abandons him.
now: You heard the reminder. A talk, a verse, a friend's honest word. Then a scroll, a laugh, a distraction, and it was gone. {idea}The danger is not missing the message. It is being talked out of it after it arrives.{/idea}
old: I heard it, so I am fine; I can come back to it.
new: Once the reminder reaches me, the next pull away is the real test.
try: After the next reminder that touches you, act on it within the hour, before anything talks you out of it.

title: My Lord, my people abandoned this Quran.
subtitle: The Messenger's complaint, and the many ways to abandon
then: The Messenger ﷺ complains to Allah that his people {trap}deserted this Quran{/trap}. The idolators would make noise when it was recited. Ibn Kathir widens it: {idea}not pondering it, not acting on it, or turning to idle talk instead{/idea} are also forms of forsaking it.
now: There is a Quran app on your phone. Last opened during Ramadan. You can name ten series you watched this year. {idea}This complaint is not only about Makkah.{/idea} It is gentle enough to reach you too.
old: I believe in the Quran, so this verse is not about me.
new: Believing in it while never reading or living it is also a way of leaving it.
try: Open the Quran today and read one page slowly, with its meaning.

title: Every prophet had an enemy. Your Lord is enough.
subtitle: Opposition is normal, and so is His help
then: Right after the Messenger ﷺ complains that his people abandoned the Quran, Allah comforts him. Ibn Kathir says {idea}in every earlier nation, each prophet had an enemy among the criminals{/idea}. The idolators tried to stop people following the Quran, so Allah says He is {reward}enough as a Guide and Helper{/reward}.
now: You start wearing hijab, or stop going to the Friday drinks, and someone at work makes it their hobby to comment. You wonder if you are doing something wrong. {idea}Resistance is part of the path, not proof you left it.{/idea}
old: If people push back this hard, maybe I am on the wrong track.
new: Opposition came to every prophet, and Allah is enough for anyone on that path.
try: The next time someone mocks a good choice you made, say to yourself: Allah is enough as a Guide and Helper.

title: Why not all at once? To steady your heart.
subtitle: Why the Quran came in stages over years
then: The disbelievers asked why the Quran did not come down all at once like the Tawrah and Injil. Ibn Kathir says it came {idea}in stages over twenty-three years, according to events{/idea}, {reward}to strengthen the hearts of the believers{/reward}. Each hard moment had its own verses.
now: You want to fix your whole life this month: prayer, diet, temper, sleep. By week two you have quit everything. {idea}Allah sent His guidance in steps{/idea}, so a heart could take it in. You can take it in the same way.
old: If I cannot change everything at once, there is no point starting.
new: Guidance came in steps to make hearts firm, and my change can come in steps too.
try: Pick one small change only. Do it every day this week before adding anything else.

title: Every objection they bring gets a truer, clearer answer.
subtitle: The Quran answers doubts with something better
then: Ibn Kathir says this covers {trap}every argument or doubt{/trap} the disbelievers raised. Whatever they said to oppose the truth, Allah answered {idea}with the truth of that same matter, more clearly and more eloquently{/idea}. This surah itself is full of such replies.
now: A video makes a clever point against your faith and it sits in your chest for days. You are afraid to look closer. {idea}The Quran was built to meet doubts face to face{/idea}, so looking for the answer is not a betrayal. It is how it was meant to work.
old: If I look into my doubts, they might win.
new: The Quran meets each objection with a clearer truth, so I can ask honestly.
try: Write down one doubt that bothers you and ask someone knowledgeable about it this week.

title: Gathered on their faces: the worst place, the farthest astray.
subtitle: How those who refused will be raised
then: After the replies to their objections, Allah describes how {trap}the deniers will be gathered on their faces{/trap}. Ibn Kathir reports that a man asked the Prophet ﷺ how this could be. He answered that {idea}the One who made him walk on two feet can make him walk on his face{/idea}.
now: You walk into the office, the gym, the mall, head up. Your feet carry you without a thought. {idea}Every step is something given.{/idea} The verse asks where you are walking with it.
old: Walking upright is just how I am built.
new: My feet and my standing are gifts, and the One who gave them can take them.
try: On one walk today, thank Allah for your feet and ask Him to guide where they go.

title: Musa was given the Book and his brother as a helper.
subtitle: Even a great prophet was given support
then: The surah now turns to past nations as a warning to Quraysh. It begins with Musa, given {idea}the Scripture{/idea}, and {reward}his brother Harun as a helper{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says Harun was another prophet who helped and supported him.
now: You are the one in the family who handles everything: the bills, the hospital visits, the forms. You do not ask for help because you think you should not need it. {reward}Allah gave Musa a brother at his side.{/reward} Needing a helper is not a weakness.
old: If I were strong enough, I would not need anyone's help.
new: Even Musa was given a helper. Support is a gift from Allah, not a failure.
try: Ask one person today to share one task you have been carrying alone.

title: Go, both of you, to the people who denied.
subtitle: Two brothers sent, and a people who refused
then: Allah told Musa and Harun to {idea}go together{/idea} to the people who denied His signs. Ibn Kathir says {trap}Pharaoh and his chiefs denied them both{/trap}, and they were destroyed. It was told to Quraysh, who were now denying a messenger too.
now: You keep getting the same reminder: from a friend, a khutbah, a verse on your feed. You roll your eyes each time. {idea}The question is not whether the message reached you. It is what you did when it did.{/idea}
old: Messages like this are for other people who need them.
new: The message came to people who denied it too. It reached me for a reason.
try: Take the reminder you have heard most often lately and act on it once today.

title: Nuh's people denied the messengers, and became a sign.
subtitle: Denying one messenger is denying them all
then: Only Nuh was sent to them, yet the verse says they denied {idea}the messengers{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains that {idea}whoever denies one messenger denies them all{/idea}, because their message is the same. Nuh called them for 950 years, and few believed. They were drowned and {reward}made a lesson{/reward}.
now: You accept the parts of the religion that fit your life and wave away the parts that cost you. It feels like a small edit. {idea}The message comes as one piece.{/idea} Picking and dropping is a quiet kind of denial.
old: I can take the parts I like and leave the rest.
new: The message is one, so refusing part of it is refusing more than I think.
try: Name one teaching you avoid because it is inconvenient. Read about why it matters today.

title: Ad, Thamud, the people of the well, and many between.
subtitle: A list longer than the names in it
then: The verse names {idea}Ad, Thamud and the people of Ar-Rass{/idea}. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abbas that Ar-Rass was one of the villages of Thamud, and from Ikrimah that it was a well. Then {idea}many generations in between{/idea}, far more than are mentioned.
now: You scroll past news about a once-famous company that collapsed. A week later you have forgotten it. {idea}History is crowded with people who were sure they would last.{/idea} The verse lists a few and says there were many more.
old: Those were other people, long ago, nothing to do with me.
new: Many generations before me lived and ended. My time is one more in the line.
try: Spend two minutes thinking about one person who has died that you knew. Ask what you want to leave behind.

title: Each was given clear examples first.
subtitle: No one was taken without a warning
then: For each nation, Allah says {idea}We put forward examples{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains this as showing them the proof and clear evidence. Qatadah said: {trap}they had no excuse{/trap}. Only then were they destroyed.
now: Your doctor told you, your spouse told you, your own body told you. Then something happens and you say it came out of nowhere. {idea}Most of the time, the examples came first.{/idea}
old: Bad outcomes come without warning.
new: Allah sends clear signs first. My job is to notice them while they are still signs.
try: List one warning sign in your life you have been ignoring. Take one step in response today.

title: They passed the ruined town and learned nothing.
subtitle: Seeing is not the same as reflecting

row.title: they did not expect the Day

then: Ibn Kathir says this is {trap}the town of the people of Lut, Sodom{/trap}, which lay on the open highway the Makkan traders used. They passed it morning and night. {idea}They did not learn a lesson{/idea}, because they did not expect any resurrection.
now: You drive past the hospital every day. You walk past the cemetery on the way to the station. {idea}Seeing it every day can make you stop seeing it at all.{/idea}
old: I have seen those reminders a hundred times, they do not mean much.
new: The reminders I pass every day only work if I stop and think about my own end.
try: Next time you pass a hospital or graveyard, slow down and make one dua for yourself and the people inside.

title: Is this the one Allah sent? they mocked.
subtitle: Mockery as a way to avoid listening

row.title: belittling
sub: so the message does not land

then: When the disbelievers saw the Prophet ﷺ, they mocked: {trap}is this the one Allah sent?{/trap} Ibn Kathir says they said it {trap}to belittle and undermine him{/trap}, looking for faults. He notes that messengers before him were mocked too.
now: Someone at the family dinner is serious about their deen, and the table turns it into a running joke. You laugh because everyone does. {idea}Laughing at the messenger is an easy way to never deal with the message.{/idea}
old: It is just a joke, nobody means anything by it.
new: Mocking is often how people protect themselves from having to listen.
try: The next time a sincere person is mocked in front of you, do not laugh along. Say one kind word instead.

title: He almost pulled us away, if we had not held firm.
subtitle: Patience in the wrong thing

row.title: a trap
sub: when it holds you in the wrong place

then: The mockers admitted something: {idea}he nearly turned us away from our idols{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains they meant he would have done it, {trap}had we not been patient and persevered in our ways{/trap}. Allah replies that they will know who was astray when they see the punishment.
now: You almost apologized to your brother. You almost quit the habit. Then you held on, and called it being strong. {trap}Stubbornness can feel like strength from the inside.{/trap}
old: Sticking to my position no matter what is a sign of character.
new: Holding firm is only good when I am holding the truth.
try: Think of one position you have refused to budge on. Ask yourself honestly if it is truth or pride.

title: Have you seen the one who made his desire his god?
subtitle: When whatever I like becomes my religion
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}whatever he admires and sees as good becomes his religion{/trap}. Ibn Abbas said that in Jahiliyyah a man would worship a white rock, then {trap}find a better-looking one and switch{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ is told he is not this man's guardian.
now: You say you follow the religion, but if a rule is inconvenient, you find a reason it does not apply to you. Next year a different rule. {trap}The rock keeps changing because the real god is what you want.{/trap}
old: I follow what feels right to me.
new: If my feelings always win over Allah's word, my feelings are what I worship.
try: Pick one thing you do only because you want to, against what you know. Say no to it once today.

title: Do they hear or think? Even cattle do better.
subtitle: Cattle do what they were made for

row.title: cattle
sub: do what they were made for

row.title: people who refuse
sub: made to worship Allah, did not

then: Allah asks whether most of them truly hear or understand. Ibn Kathir explains why they are {trap}farther astray than cattle{/trap}: {idea}cattle only do what they were created to do{/idea}. These people were created to worship Allah alone, had messengers and proof, and still did otherwise.
now: Wake, scroll, work, eat, scroll, sleep. Weeks go by like this. You hear the adhan from your phone and swipe it away. {idea}You are made for more than grazing.{/idea}
old: Living comfortably day to day is enough.
new: I was made for a purpose, and ignoring it puts me below what animals manage.
try: Today, when the call to prayer comes, stop what you are doing and pray on time.

title: Look how your Lord stretches the shadow.
subtitle: A sign you can watch every morning

row.title: He moves it
sub: He could have kept it still

then: Now the surah turns from the deniers to signs in nature. Many early scholars said the spread shadow is {idea}the time from dawn until sunrise{/idea}. If Allah willed, it would stay still forever. {idea}The sun is its guide{/idea}, and a thing is known by its opposite, Ibn Kathir says.
now: You are up early for Fajr, or a shift, or a crying baby. The light is grey and soft and the shadows are long. {idea}That quiet hour is a sign being shown to you{/idea}, if you look up from your phone.
old: Morning light is just the start of another busy day.
new: The changing shadows are my Lord at work, shown to me every single day.
try: Tomorrow at dawn, look outside for one minute and watch the light before you check your phone.

title: Then He draws the shadow back, little by little.
subtitle: A slow withdrawal you barely notice
then: Continuing the sign of the shadow, Allah says He {idea}withdraws it towards Himself, gradually{/idea}. As-Suddi described it as {idea}a gentle, concealed withdrawal{/idea} until no shade is left except under a roof or a tree. Ayyub bin Musa said: little by little.
now: Your child is suddenly taller than you. Your father's hair is suddenly white. It was never sudden. {idea}Allah moves things gently enough that you miss it{/idea}, unless you stop and watch.
old: Nothing much changes from one day to the next.
new: Everything is moving quietly under His control, the way a shadow shrinks without a sound.
try: Look at one shadow at two times today and notice how far it moved. Say SubhanAllah.

title: Night as a covering, sleep as rest, day as rising.
subtitle: Every night is a small death, every morning a raising
then: Ibn Kathir says the night {idea}covers and conceals all things{/idea}. Sleep is a halt to movement, because limbs tire from working all day. {reward}It renews both body and soul.{/reward} Then the day is a rising, when people go out to earn. He links it to 28:73.
now: You push sleep back for one more episode, one more email. You treat it as the enemy of getting things done. {reward}Allah calls it rest He made for you{/reward}, and waking each morning a small resurrection.
old: Sleep is what I give up to get more done.
new: Sleep is a mercy from Allah, and each morning He raises me again.
try: Tonight, put the phone away ten minutes early and sleep with the intention of renewing yourself for good.

title: Winds come first as good news, then pure water.
subtitle: Mercy announces itself before it arrives
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the winds {idea}bring the clouds behind them{/idea}. Some form clouds, some carry them, some come ahead as heralds, some seed the rain. The water sent down is {reward}pure and purifying{/reward}, and he cites the hadith that water is pure and nothing makes it impure.
now: A cool wind before a summer storm. You feel it on your face as you rush to bring the washing in. {idea}Allah calls that wind good news{/idea}, a mercy arriving before the mercy.
old: Wind and rain are just the forecast.
new: The wind before rain is Allah sending good news ahead of His mercy.
try: The next time you feel wind before rain, stop and thank Allah for the mercy coming.

title: Rain brings a dead land to life and gives drink.
subtitle: From bare ground to flowers
then: Ibn Kathir describes {trap}a land that waited a long time for rain{/trap}, with nothing on it. When rain comes, {reward}its hills are covered with colorful flowers{/reward}. Animals drink, and people in desperate need water their crops. He links it to 41:39 and 30:50.
now: Your heart feels dry. It has been months since prayer felt like anything. You assume that part of you has died. {reward}A dead land is only waiting.{/reward} The same Lord who sends the rain can bring it back.
old: My faith has dried up, and it is not coming back.
new: Allah brings dead land to life with one rain, and He can do that for my heart.
try: Ask Allah today, in your own words, to bring your heart back to life.

title: He spreads the rain around so people remember.
subtitle: Rain here, none there, and who gets the thanks
then: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud said {idea}one year does not have more rain than another, Allah distributes it as He wills{/idea}. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith where Allah says of those who credited the rain to a star: {trap}disbelievers in Me{/trap}, and of those who said {reward}by the mercy of Allah{/reward}: believers.
now: Payday comes, and you say the company finally paid. The contract comes, and you say it was your networking. {idea}The rain still comes from somewhere, even when you name a star.{/idea}
old: Good things come from the system, the market, my effort.
new: Whatever reaches me arrives by the mercy of Allah, and I want to say so.
try: The next good thing that happens today, say out loud: this is from the mercy of Allah.

title: He could have sent a warner to every town.
subtitle: One messenger for all people
then: Allah could have raised a warner in every town. Ibn Kathir says He instead {idea}singled out Muhammad ﷺ to be sent to all the people of earth{/idea}. He cites 6:19: that I may warn you {idea}and whomever it may reach{/idea}. And the hadith: I have been sent to the red and the black.
now: You read this on a phone, in a city and a century the Prophet ﷺ never saw. {idea}You are one of the whoever it may reach.{/idea} The message did not need a new warner for your town. It already arrived.
old: The Quran was mainly for the people back then.
new: I am among those it was meant to reach. It is speaking to me.
try: Read one verse today as if it were sent directly to you, and write down what it asks of you.

title: Do not obey them. Strive with the Quran.
subtitle: The tool for the struggle was the Book itself
then: This was revealed in Makkah, when the Prophet ﷺ and the believers were few and under pressure. Allah tells him {trap}not to obey the disbelievers{/trap}. Ibn Abbas said the striving here is {idea}with the Quran{/idea}: conveying it, reciting it, standing by it with full effort.
now: Everyone in your circle thinks your values are old-fashioned, and you feel the pull to soften. {idea}The answer is not to get louder. It is to hold the Quran closer{/idea} and let it shape what you say and do.
old: To stand firm I need to win every argument.
new: Holding to the Quran with real effort is the struggle, and it is enough.
try: When you feel pressure to give up a value today, recite one verse you know by heart before you reply.

title: Sweet water and salt water, kept apart by Him.
subtitle: Two kinds of water, each for its purpose

row.title: a protection
sub: keeps the air and earth healthy

then: Ibn Kathir says this is {reward}the sweet water flowing among people{/reward}, portioned out by Allah to each land as it needs, and {idea}the salt seas{/idea}. He says Allah made the seas salty {idea}lest the air turn putrid{/idea}. Between them He set a barrier of dry land so one does not overrun the other.
now: You fill a glass from the tap without a thought. Millions live near the sea and still need fresh water. {reward}The sweet water in your glass was portioned to you{/reward}, and kept apart from the salt so you could drink.
old: Clean water is just a utility I pay for.
new: Every glass of fresh water is portioned and protected for me by Allah.
try: Drink your next glass of water slowly, sitting, and say Alhamdulillah after it.

title: From water He made a person, then family by blood and marriage.
subtitle: A web of relatives from one small beginning
then: Ibn Kathir says man was created {idea}from a weak drop, then shaped and formed{/idea}. Then: {idea}in the beginning he is someone's child, then he marries and becomes a son-in-law{/idea}, then has in-laws of his own. All this from a humble liquid. Your Lord is able to do what He wills.
now: The family group chat is noisy. Your in-laws can be a lot. Your cousin never replies. {idea}Every one of those ties was appointed by Allah{/idea}, woven out of a drop of water.
old: My relatives are just people I happen to be connected to.
new: My family by blood and by marriage is something Allah built around me.
try: Message one relative, by blood or marriage, that you have not spoken to in a while.

title: They worship what cannot help or harm them.
subtitle: And end up working against their own Lord
then: After all these signs, the verse returns to the idolators. Ibn Kathir says they worshipped idols {trap}with no evidence, led only by whims{/trap}, and fought to protect them. Mujahid said the disbeliever {trap}helps Satan in disobedience to Allah{/trap}.
now: You defend a habit you know is wrong, getting angry when someone questions it. You stand up for it like it deserves protecting. {trap}Defending what harms you puts you on its side.{/trap}
old: I am not against Allah, I just do my own thing.
new: When I defend what Allah dislikes, I am taking a side, even quietly.
try: Notice one thing you got defensive about this week. Ask whether it deserves your defense.

title: Sent only to bring good news and to warn.
subtitle: The Prophet's role, in two parts
then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ what he was sent for. Ibn Kathir explains: {reward}a bringer of good news of Paradise to those who obey{/reward}, and {trap}a warner of punishment to those who go against Allah's commands{/trap}. Not to force anyone, just to tell them.
now: You remember religion from childhood as a list of things that would get you punished. {reward}Half the message is good news{/reward}, and it was always meant to come first, together with the warning.
old: Religion is mostly about what I will be punished for.
new: The Prophet ﷺ came with good news and warning, and I need to hear both.
try: Look up one hadith of good news today and share it with someone who needs hope.

title: I ask no payment. Just take a path to your Lord.
subtitle: A messenger with nothing to sell
then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to say: {idea}I ask no reward for this{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains, not from your wealth, {idea}I do this only for the sake of Allah{/idea}. The only thing he wanted was that {reward}whoever wills takes a path to his Lord{/reward}.
now: Every app wants your data, every influencer has a code, every advice comes with a course to buy. {idea}This message asks for nothing except that you walk toward Allah.{/idea}
old: Everyone telling me what to do wants something from me.
new: The Prophet ﷺ wanted nothing from me except my own good with my Lord.
try: Do one good thing for someone today and expect nothing back, not even thanks.

title: Rely on the Living One who never dies.
subtitle: Trust, praise, and a Lord who knows every sin
then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to {idea}put his trust in the Ever-Living who never dies{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says He will be sufficient and a helper. Then: glorify Him with praise. The Prophet ﷺ used to say {reward}Glory be to You, O Allah, and with Your praise{/reward}. And He knows His servants' sins fully.
now: Your father was your rock, and then the hospital corridor, the phone call. Everything you leaned on shook. {reward}The One you can lean on fully will never get that phone call.{/reward}
old: I am secure as long as the people I depend on are here.
new: Everyone I lean on will die, except Allah. He is the One to rely on.
try: Say SubhanAllahi wa bihamdihi a few times today when you feel anxious about something.

title: The Most Merciful made it all. Ask one who knows Him.
subtitle: Learning about Allah from the best-informed
then: Allah describes Himself as Creator of the heavens and earth in six days, who {idea}then rose over the Throne{/idea}, running all affairs. Then: ask one well-informed. Ibn Kathir says {idea}no one knows more about Allah than His Messenger ﷺ{/idea}, so follow him in what he taught.
now: You have a question about Allah, and you type it into a search bar at 1am and take the first answer. {idea}The verse says ask the one who knows{/idea}: go to what the Prophet ﷺ taught, through people who learned it properly.
old: Anyone's opinion about Allah is as good as anyone else's.
new: To learn about the Most Merciful, I go to the one who knew Him best.
try: Write down one question you have about Allah and ask a trusted, learned person this week.

title: Bow to the Most Merciful? And what is that?
subtitle: When even a gentle name pushes people away
then: When told to prostrate to Ar-Rahman, they said: {trap}what is Ar-Rahman?{/trap} Ibn Kathir says they disliked that name, as at Hudaybiyyah when they refused to write In the Name of Allah, Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim. {trap}The invitation only increased their aversion.{/trap}
now: Someone younger reminds you to pray, and something in you bristles. You would have done it, but not because they told you. {trap}Sometimes it is the messenger we resist, not the message.{/trap}
old: I will do it, just not because that person told me to.
new: The call is to bow to the Most Merciful. Who delivers it should not stop me.
try: Next time someone reminds you of something good, thank them and do it, even if their tone bothered you.

title: Great stars, a burning lamp, and a moon that glows.
subtitle: The sky as a sign of His blessing

picture.label: What He placed in the sky

then: Allah praises Himself for the beauty He placed in the sky. Ibn Kathir says Al-Buruj are {idea}the giant stars{/idea}, the lamp is {idea}the sun{/idea}, and the moon gives light {reward}illuminated by something else, different from the sun's light{/reward}. He links it to 10:5 and to Nuh's words in 71:15-16.
now: You step out of the car late at night and the moon is huge over the car park. You glance and go inside. {idea}The verse opens with Blessed is He{/idea}, asking you to stay and look a little longer.
old: The sky is just there, I have seen it a thousand times.
new: Every star, the sun and the moon were placed by Him, and they call me to praise Him.
try: Tonight, step outside for one minute, look at the sky, and say Tabarak Allah.

title: Night and day take turns, for whoever wants to remember.
subtitle: A second chance built into every day

row.title: make it up
sub: night after day, day after night

then: Ibn Kathir says the night and day {idea}follow one another so servants know the times of worship{/idea}. Whoever misses something at night can make it up by day, and the other way. He cites the hadith: {reward}Allah spreads His Hand at night for the one who did wrong by day to repent{/reward}, and by day for the one who did wrong by night.
now: You lost your temper at work, skipped your prayers, and went to bed feeling like a failure. {reward}The night was already a door held open{/reward}, and the morning is another one.
old: Today went badly, so I have ruined it.
new: Night and day keep replacing each other so I can always turn back.
try: Before sleeping tonight, ask forgiveness for one thing from today, then sleep in peace.

title: They walk gently, and answer insults with peace.
subtitle: The first marks of the servants of the Most Merciful

picture.label: The servants of the Most Merciful

then: After all the objections, the surah now shows what the believers look like. Ibn Kathir says they walk {idea}with dignity and humility, not arrogance{/idea}. It does not mean walking like a sick person. When the foolish insult them, {reward}they forgive, overlook, and say only good{/reward}, as the Prophet ﷺ did.
now: A driver cuts you off and gestures at you through the window. Someone leaves a rude comment on your post. Your thumb is already typing the reply. {idea}The servants of the Most Merciful say peace and move on.{/idea}
old: If I do not hit back, they will think I am weak.
new: Answering rudeness with calm is strength the Most Merciful loves in His servants.
try: The next time someone is rude to you today, do not reply in kind. Say something calm or say nothing.

title: Their nights are spent bowing and standing for their Lord.
subtitle: What the servants do when no one sees
then: Ibn Kathir says {reward}their nights are the best of nights{/reward}, spent in worship and obedience. He links it to 51:17, {idea}they slept little by night and asked forgiveness before dawn{/idea}, and to 32:16, their sides forsake their beds.
now: Your day belongs to the job, the kids, the commute. The night belongs to the phone. {reward}A few minutes of the night given to Allah{/reward}, when the house is quiet, can be the most honest part of your day.
old: Night prayer is for very pious people, not for someone like me.
new: Even two short units of prayer at night make my night part of that night.
try: Tonight, pray two short units before sleeping, or set an alarm for ten minutes before Fajr.

title: Even after night prayer, they ask to be saved.
subtitle: Worship without self-satisfaction
then: The same people who spend the night in prayer still say: {idea}Our Lord, avert from us the torment of Hell{/idea}. Al-Hasan explained the word for clinging: {trap}whatever strikes a person and then passes is not that; it is what lasts{/trap}. Their worship did not make them feel safe from it.
now: You had a good Ramadan, gave in charity, prayed on time for a month. A quiet thought arrives: I am one of the good ones now. {idea}The servants of the Most Merciful pray and still ask.{/idea}
old: I have done a lot of good, so I am safe.
new: The more I worship, the more I ask Allah to save me, not the less.
try: After your next prayer, ask Allah sincerely to protect you from the Fire.

title: An evil place to settle and to stay.
subtitle: Why they keep asking

picture.label: What they ask to be kept from

then: The servants' prayer continues: {trap}it is evil as an abode and as a place to rest{/trap}. Ibn Kathir explains, how evil it looks as a dwelling and as a place to stay. The surah keeps placing two homes side by side, and {reward}the servants know which one they want{/reward}.
now: You spend months comparing flats, reading reviews, checking the area. You care a lot about where you will live. {idea}The servants care that much about the last home too{/idea}, and they ask for it in their prayers.
old: I will think about where I end up when I get older.
new: I put effort into where I live here. My final home deserves more.
try: Ask Allah tonight for a good final home, in the same words you would use for something you really want.

title: When they spend, neither wasteful nor stingy, but balanced.
subtitle: Money handled in the middle way
then: Ibn Kathir says they are {trap}not extravagant, spending more than they need{/trap}, nor {trap}miserly toward their families{/trap}. They follow the fairest way. {idea}The best of matters are those which are moderate.{/idea} He links it to 17:29.
now: Payday. The online cart is full by evening. Or the opposite: you save every penny and your kids go without things they actually need. {idea}The verse puts the servant in the middle{/idea}, with a hand neither tied nor fully open.
old: Being good with money means spending as little as possible, or I deserve to treat myself.
new: The servant of the Most Merciful spends in balance: enough for needs, without waste.
try: Look at your last week of spending. Find one waste to cut and one need you have been neglecting.

title: They keep away from three great wrongs.
subtitle: No partner with Allah, no unjust killing, no zina

row.title: unjust killing
sub: of a soul He made sacred

then: Ibn Mas'ud said the Prophet ﷺ was asked which sin is greatest. He said: {trap}that you set up a rival to Allah when He created you{/trap}, then killing one's child, then adultery with a neighbor's wife, and this verse came confirming it. Ibn Abbas reported that people who had done these came asking {reward}if there was a way back{/reward}.
now: Most of us will never take a life. But you can see how the big wrongs begin small: a loyalty given to something above Allah, a glance that becomes a chat, anger allowed to grow. {idea}The servants guard the edges, not only the cliff.{/idea}
old: I would never do those things, so this verse is not for me.
new: The great sins start with small steps, and the servants avoid the steps too.
try: Identify one small step in your life that leads toward something serious. Close it today.

title: For those who persist, the punishment is doubled.
subtitle: The seriousness, said plainly before the door opens
then: Ibn Kathir explains the punishment for these sins as {trap}repeated and intensified, in disgrace{/trap}. But the very next verse begins {reward}except those who repent{/reward}. He calls it evidence that even the repentance of a murderer is accepted.
now: A doctor tells you the scan is serious, then says: but there is a treatment. You need both sentences. {idea}The weight is said plainly so the way out means something.{/idea}
old: Hearing how serious sin is makes me want to give up.
new: The seriousness is shown so I take the way back seriously, and it is right there.
try: If something heavy weighs on you, read the next verse, 25:70, slowly today.

title: Repent, believe, do good, and He turns sins into good deeds.
subtitle: The most hopeful exception
then: Abu Dharr narrated that a man will be shown his minor sins and told: {reward}for every evil deed you now have a good one{/reward}. He will say, O Lord, I did things I do not see here, and {reward}the Prophet ﷺ smiled{/reward}. An old man asked if even his betrayals could be forgiven. He was told: even your betrayals.
now: There is something in your past you never tell anyone. It replays in your head at 3am. {reward}Allah does not only erase it for the one who repents. He replaces it with good.{/reward}
old: What I did is too much; I can only hope it is ignored.
new: If I truly turn back, Allah can turn my worst deeds into good ones.
try: Make one honest repentance today for a thing you have kept hidden, then do one good deed after it.

title: Whoever repents and does good has truly turned to Allah.
subtitle: Repentance that is accepted, for any sin
then: Ibn Kathir says this shows {reward}His mercy extends to all His creatures{/reward}: whoever repents, He accepts it {reward}for any sin, great or small{/reward}. He links it to 4:110, 9:104 and 39:53, despair not of the mercy of Allah.
now: You have repented before and slipped again. You feel embarrassed to ask one more time. {idea}Turning back with good deeds is what makes it real{/idea}, and the door does not close because you came back again.
old: I have asked forgiveness too many times; it does not count anymore.
new: Every sincere turning back, followed by good, is accepted by Allah.
try: After asking forgiveness today, follow it with one specific good action within the hour.

title: They do not witness falsehood, and pass idle talk with dignity.
subtitle: Where the servants refuse to be present
then: Ibn Kathir says they do not bear witness to falsehood: {trap}lies, immorality, foul speech{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ warned against false speech and false testimony, {trap}repeating it until the Companions wished he would stop{/trap}. When they pass by idle talk, {idea}they do not let it touch them{/idea}.
now: The break-room conversation turns into mocking a colleague who is not there. You do not join in, but you stay and laugh. {idea}Being in the room is being a witness.{/idea} The servants find a way to leave with dignity.
old: I did not say anything bad, I was just there.
new: Where I choose to stay is part of what I testify to.
try: The next time a conversation turns to gossip or mockery, change the subject or walk away calmly.

title: Reminded of His verses, they do not fall deaf and blind.
subtitle: Letting the verses actually reach you
then: Ibn Kathir contrasts them with those who hear the words of Allah and {trap}are not moved to change their ways, as if deaf and blind{/trap}. The servants are like those in 8:2: {idea}when His verses are recited, their faith increases{/idea}.
now: The Quran plays in the car on the way to work while you answer messages at red lights. It is on, but you are not there. {idea}The servants let it in.{/idea} Even one verse heard properly can turn the day.
old: I listen to Quran a lot, so I am fine.
new: Hearing it is not enough. The servants let the verses change them.
try: Listen to one short surah today with nothing else in your hands, and notice one thing it asks of you.

title: Our Lord, give us spouses and children who cool our eyes.
subtitle: A dua for family and for leading in good

key.label: What comfort of the eyes is

then: Ibn Abbas said it means {reward}offspring who strive to obey Allah and bring joy in this world and the next{/reward}. Al-Miqdad said believers who saw loved ones refuse faith could not rest, and this dua was for that. Asking to be leaders means {idea}examples in good{/idea}, so guidance reaches beyond themselves.
now: You worry about your teenager's friends, your marriage after a hard year, the baby who will not sleep. {reward}This is the dua for all of it{/reward}: not just that they are fine, but that they bring joy that reaches the Hereafter.
old: My family will turn out fine if I work hard and provide well.
new: The comfort I really want in my family is a gift I have to ask Allah for.
try: Memorize this dua today and say it for your family after one prayer.

title: The high chamber is theirs because they were patient.
subtitle: Greeted with peace at the end
then: After listing the servants' traits, Allah names the reward: {reward}the high chamber{/reward}, named for its elevation. Ibn Kathir says it is {idea}because of their patience in doing what they did{/idea}. They will be met {reward}with words of welcome, honor, and peace{/reward}.
now: Answering rudeness with calm, waking for night prayer, spending in balance, walking out of the gossip. None of it is flashy. {idea}All of it takes patience.{/idea} That is exactly what the verse says is rewarded.
old: These small efforts do not add up to much.
new: The patience in my small daily efforts is what earns the high place.
try: Choose one trait from verses 63-74 and practice it patiently today.

title: Forever there: a beautiful home and a place to rest.
subtitle: The home they will never want to leave
then: Ibn Kathir says they will {reward}settle there and never leave, move or die{/reward}, and never wish to move elsewhere. The words mirror verse 66: they had asked to be kept from {trap}an evil settlement{/trap}, and they receive {reward}an excellent one{/reward}.
now: You have moved four times in six years. Leases end, rent goes up, jobs change cities. {reward}The verse promises a home you will never have to pack up{/reward}, and never want to.
old: Nowhere really feels permanent.
new: The permanent home is promised, and every patient step points toward it.
try: Next time you feel unsettled about where you live, ask Allah for the home that never ends.

title: My Lord would not care for you, if not for your prayer.
subtitle: The surah ends on what makes us matter
then: The surah closes with a word to the deniers of Makkah. Ibn Kathir says {idea}He would not pay attention to you if you did not worship Him, for He created mankind to worship Him alone{/idea}. Their denial would stay with them. Ibn Mas'ud and others linked it to Badr; Al-Hasan to the Day of Resurrection.
now: You measure your worth by your job title, your follower count, what your family thinks. Some days you feel invisible. {idea}What makes you matter to Allah is that you call on Him.{/idea} Every dua is you being seen.
old: I matter because of what I achieve and who notices.
new: I matter to my Lord because I turn to Him and call on Him.
try: Make one dua today just to talk to Allah, with nothing to ask for but nearness to Him.
